title: Ezekiel 1:22–28
context: The prophet’s gaze rises. Over the heads of the living creatures is “the likeness of an expanse, like an awesome crystal to look at” (1:22). Under it the creatures’ wings are straight, and their noise is “like the noise of great waters, like the voice of the Almighty,” and like an army; then “There was a voice above the expanse” (1:23–25). Above the expanse is “the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone”, and on it “a likeness as the appearance of a man” (1:26), with glowing metal, fire, and brightness all around like the rainbow in the cloud (1:27–28). The prophet sums it up with layered restraint: “This was the appearance of the likeness of the LORD’s glory” (1:28). He falls on his face and hears a voice, which leads into the commission of chapter 2. This page follows the text’s careful language and does not attempt to picture more than the prophet says. Comparisons with Exodus 24:10 (sapphire under the feet of the God of Israel) and Revelation 4:2–3 (a throne with a rainbow around it) are noted only in passing. Both traditions read the vision as shared ground: the LORD’s glory is sovereign and holy, and it appears to exiles.

verses.text: Over the head of the living creature there was the likeness of an expanse, like an awesome crystal to look at, stretched out over their heads above.
verses.arminianNotes: Over their heads is “the likeness of an expanse, like an awesome crystal to look at”. Arminian readers note the word “expanse,” which also appears in the creation account (compare Genesis 1:6). The vision draws on the language of the heavens above the earth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the expanse as a boundary between the creatures below and the throne above, marking the distance between servants and their Lord. Shared ground: both traditions read the crystal expanse as part of the vision’s ascending order and hedge any further symbolism.

verses.text: Under the expanse, their wings were straight, one toward the other. Each one had two which covered on this side, and each one had two which covered their bodies on that side.
verses.arminianNotes: “Under the expanse, their wings were straight,” and each creature had two wings covering its body. Arminian readers note the reverent stillness beneath the throne. The creatures that move with such power also keep a posture of covering before the one above them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see reverence in the covering wings, consistent with 1:11. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing the description beneath the expanse, and neither presses a doctrine from the arrangement of the wings.

verses.text: When they went, I heard the noise of their wings like the noise of great waters, like the voice of the Almighty, a noise of tumult like the noise of an army. When they stood, they let down their wings.
verses.arminianNotes: The noise of their wings was “like the noise of great waters, like the voice of the Almighty,” and like an army. Arminian readers note how the prophet reaches for overwhelming sounds. The holy presence is heard as well as seen, and it is not tame.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the majesty of God conveyed through sound, echoing “the voice of the Almighty”. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as awe before God’s power, and both note that the wings are let down when the creatures stand, preparing for the voice in 1:25.

verses.text: There was a voice above the expanse that was over their heads. When they stood, they let down their wings.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was a voice above the expanse that was over their heads.” Arminian readers note that the vision is not mere spectacle; it is the setting for speech. The LORD will address the prophet, and the visible glory serves the word that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priority of the word in the vision: the creatures let down their wings, and the voice from above is heard. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as pointing ahead to the commission in 2:1, where the voice speaks to the prophet directly.

verses.text: Above the expanse that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone. On the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a man on it above.
verses.arminianNotes: Above the expanse is “the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone”, and on it “a likeness as the appearance of a man”. Arminian readers note the layered hedging and see the LORD enthroned over exiles. Some Christian readers have seen here a hint of the incarnation, held with care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress the careful “likeness” language and center the verse on God’s enthroned rule. Some, like other Christian readers, have connected the human likeness with the incarnation, offered as a reading rather than the text’s claim. Shared ground: both mention Exodus 24:10 only in passing.

verses.text: I saw as it were glowing metal, as the appearance of fire within it all around, from the appearance of his waist and upward; and from the appearance of his waist and downward I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and there was brightness around him.
verses.arminianNotes: Upward and downward from “the appearance of his waist” the prophet sees glowing metal and fire, with brightness around him. Arminian readers note that the description never becomes a portrait. The fire both reveals and conceals, and the prophet keeps his distance in words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise stress that God’s glory exceeds every description, so the prophet speaks only of appearances. Shared ground: both traditions read the fire and brightness as holiness and majesty, and both decline to fill in what the prophet does not describe.

verses.text: As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of the LORD’s glory. When I saw it, I fell on my face, and I heard a voice of one that spoke.
verses.arminianNotes: The brightness is like “the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain,” and the prophet calls it “the appearance of the likeness of the LORD’s glory.” He falls on his face. Arminian readers note that some hear an echo of the rainbow in Genesis 9:13, a link held lightly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the threefold hedge in “the appearance of the likeness” of the glory, and see in the prophet’s falling down the fitting response to God’s majesty. Shared ground: both traditions read worshipful awe here and mention the rainbow of Revelation 4:3 only in passing.
